items.title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
items.summary: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.
items.content:
Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder

Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old.

Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition.

Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day.

"I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC.

"I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't."

Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words.

It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week.

The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommender content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow.

It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality.

Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws – which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services – will help Australians become happier and healthier.

But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech.

Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral.

Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago.

It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric.

He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order.

"You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC.

"I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character."

The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay.

Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man."

Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor.

Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see – and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users.

Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools.

But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture.

Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction , external ; that algorithms – often unsolicited – serve up content which harms users' mental health , external , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline .

Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line.

"The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC.

While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change.

"Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them.

Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s – a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite.

More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts.

The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off.

"This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said.

"If people want to doom scroll… that's fine, that's up to them."

Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears

The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services – social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more – to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment".

Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features – for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women – and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (£52m, $70m).

"The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC.

There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation.

In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive – although a US jury recently ruled otherwise .

"I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' – like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' – and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney.

Right-wing parties in Australia – and the Trump administration – have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship.

But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake – they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week.

The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children.

However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued.

The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 – after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds – is a cautionary tale.

Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that.

"Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation , external .

On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return.

items.summary: Article URL: https://www.arrl.org/arrlletterissue?issue=2026-10-15#eBay-Restricts-Listings-of-Radio-Equipment_-But-Exempts-Ham-Band-Only-Gear Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50122034 Points: 148 # Comments: 125
items.content:
Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias

eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear

Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias

Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm.

In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable.

Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions.

"While traditional communications systems have become significantly more reliable over the years, amateur radio continues to serve as a dependable auxiliary communications resource," said Arc Thames, W4CPD, Santa Rosa County Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) Program Manager. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities."

Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide.

"During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. We always hope we're not needed, but we're glad to be there just in case when all else fails." — Thanks to ARRL Northern Florida SEC Arc Thames, W4CPD, for the above

eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear

Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies . The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products.

In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy.

In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement:

eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios. However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification. If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing.

It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization.

The Radio Club of America has brought together both wireless industry professionals and amateur radio operators for more than 100 years. Each year, it bestows prestigious awards and elevates several members to RCA Fellows. This year, as always, many of those on the list are hams. The award recipients include Dr. Charles C. Counselman, III, W1HIS, who developed technology for making highly accurate GPS positioning widely available; Jay Adrick, K8CJY, who helped develop digital television and serves as Board President of the National Voice of America Museum of Broadcasting; inventor Charles Kirmuss, WØCBK, who developed digital video and audio recording systems for public safety; Carole Perry Young Professional Award winner and electrical engineer Audrey McElroy, KM4BUN, a longtime proponent of youth in amateur radio; Dr. Ajay Poddar, AC2KG, an internationally-recognized leader in radio science and engineering; Dr. Henry Richter, W6VZA (SK), who developed the communications system for Explorer 1, the first US Earth satellite; and Anthony Rizi, NR1Z, a military and cybersecurity professional and college professor who is also active in ARISS, the Amateur Radio on the International Space Station program.

This year’s class of RCA Fellows include amateurs Rachel Jones, KO4HLC; Geoffrey Mendenhall, W8GNM; Nick Pennance, N1CKP, and Dominic “Nick” Tusa, K5EF. The award winners and new Fellows will be formally recognized at RCA’s 2026 Technical Symposium and Awards Banquet in New York City on November 21. Visit the club’s website for a complete list of awardees and their biographies .

Back in the earliest days of the internet, a whole block of IP (internet protocol) addresses — beginning with 44 — was set aside for amateur radio use. Most of that block of addresses is still there and is managed by ARDC, Amateur Radio Digital Communications. In December of 2025, ARDC launched 44Net Connect, a service intended to make it easy for hams to begin using 44Net addresses for such things as experimenting with digital modes, improving repeater infrastructure, setting up a home lab, and more. In the ensuing months, more than 2000 users have signed up and ARDC is now expanding access by doubling its number of “points of presence,” or “PoPs” around the world, adding new ones in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Sydney, Australia (current ones are in Frankfurt, Toronto, and Dallas). A PoP is a physical access point that connects different networks. “The additional PoPs will expand network capacity and bring nodes closer to users in different parts of the world,” explained Rebecca Key, KO4KVG, ARDC’s Communications Manager. “This can shorten the distance data travels, reducing latency, and improving the overall experience.”

“44Net Connect gives licensed hams a simpler way to get a static 44Net IP address without a complicated setup,” adds Key. “We’re seeing it used for everything from personal tinkering to club projects, education, and EmComm.”

You can find more information about 44Net Connect, including how to get started, in ARDC’s introductory blog post .

Mel Parkes, NM7P, has resigned as Vice Director of the ARRL Rocky Mountain Division, effective October 10, 2026. Parkes was elected in 2025 to a three-year term that began January 1, 2026. He cited health and personal reasons for his resignation.

Previously, Parkes served as Utah Section Manager for 22 years, from 1999 until 2021.

ARRL President Rick Roderick, K5UR, has appointed Ed James, KA8JMW, of Edgewood, New Mexico, to be the new Vice Director, serving the remainder of Parkes’ term, which runs through December 31, 2028. An ARRL Life Member, James has served in multiple ARRL Field Organization positions, including Section Manager of New Mexico.

ARRL is governed by an all-volunteer Board of Directors. Elections are held annually for five of ARRL’s 15 Divisions, with Directors and Vice Directors serving 3-year terms.

items.title: RetroBox Modem è il progetto perfetto per i nostalgici degli albori del Web
items.summary: Estetica anni Novanta e tutti quei bei suoni che facevano i modem dell'epoca.
items.content:
Se qualcuno ha nostalgia dei tempi in cui internet non funzionava se qualcuno parlava al telefono - e faceva anche parecchio rumore quando si attivava (perché no, non era 24/7, a meno di essere veramente, veramente ricchi), un appassionato di elettronica ha il progetto basato su Raspberry Pi che fa al caso vostro: si chiama RetroBox Modem, ed è un vero e proprio modem fai-da-te Wi-Fi, compatibile con lo standard Hayes e pensato per accedere ai servizi BBS (Bulletin Board System, altro pezzo fondamentale della preistoria del Web) ancora attivi.

A differenza dei semplici adattatori seriali-Wi-Fi, il dispositivo riproduce diversi comportamenti dei modem tradizionali, compresi i comandi AT, le sequenze di composizione del numero, gli indicatori di stato della connessione e i caratteristici suoni della negoziazione. Alla base di tutto il progetto troviamo un Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, che gestisce la connessione Wi-Fi, le comunicazioni di rete e l'interprete dei comandi Hayes. Il computer collegato invia istruzioni come AT e ATD attraverso una porta seriale; RetroBox le traduce in connessioni TCP/Telnet, consentendo di raggiungere i BBS senza bisogno di una vera linea telefonica.

items.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/designing-efficient-quantum-circuits Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50121939 Points: 86 # Comments: 18
items.content:
Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.

This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv .

Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in qubits, which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as superposition —which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits. 1

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classical algorithms , so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum circuits . These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2).

In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.

These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs.

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself n times, find n . For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

items.title: Timex, arrivano cinque nuovi orologi dedicati a Harry Potter
items.summary: Ecco prezzi e immagini.
items.content:
Sembra che Timex ci stia prendendo gusto con gli orologi in collaborazione con franchise e brand famosi della cultura popolare: nelle scorse ore ha annunciato una nuova collezione di cinque orologi dedicati a Harry Potter, ampliando un'iniziativa che aveva già portato sul mercato diversi modelli in passato. Ci sono sia proposte più classiche sia quelle più sportive avventurose, e richiamano alcuni degli elementi più riconoscibili della saga, tra cui la GiraTempo, la Pietra Filosofale e anche gli occhiali di Harry stesso.

In effetti proprio la GiraTempo è la principale protagonista della collaborazione, visto che il suo design è ripreso da tre dei cinque modelli. Il più costoso è il Q Timex Time Turner Chronograph, un cronografo da 40 mm con cassa in acciaio inossidabile, proposto a 339€. Il quadrante argentato presenta aperture a forma di stella e contatori cronografici neri disposti in modo da richiamare una clessidra. La lunetta fissa color oro è incisa con testi tratti dai libri.

Molto simile è il Q Timex Time Turner da 36 mm, che oltre ad avere un diametro inferiore è sprovvisto di tutto il sottosistema cronografo, sostituito da una piccola clessidra con glitter argentati al centro del quadrante nero e dorato. L'orologio è completato da una lunetta nera bidirezionale e da un cinturino in pelle nera prodotto da S.B. Foot Tanning Company; costa 229€. items.title: Sbobba AI nella remaster di Total War Shogun 2, SEGA la ritira dalla vendita
items.summary: La società promette che sistemerà le cose.
items.content:
Sega ha ritirato temporaneamente dalla vendita la Complete Edition di Total War: Shogun 2, la remaster del celebre strategico del 2011, a causa delle forti polemiche da parte della community per la presenza di immagini generate con l'AI - in particolare, i fan contestano l'uso di quelli che sono evidentemente algoritmi di upscaling per convertire in 4K le carte delle varie unità, che in origine erano disegnate a mano: l'algoritmo ha rimosso molti dettagli, ne ha peggiorati altri e in generale ha rovinato il feeling "umano" originale. È anche emerso che la società non ha sistemato alcuni dei bug storici più fastidiosi.

La remaster, che soprattutto riunisce in un unico pacchetto le campagne che in origine furono distribuite separatamente, era stata pubblicata appena qualche giorno fa. In un messaggio pubblicato sui propri canali social ufficiali, Sega ha riconosciuto che il risultato non soddisfa né le aspettative degli utenti né gli standard qualitativi dell'azienda. La società ha dichiarato di aver preso in considerazione commenti, segnalazioni e recensioni, e di essere al lavoro con lo studio che si è occupato materialmente del lavoro per "identificare le cause dei problemi" e sistemarli. Per il momento non sono state promesse tempistiche precise, ma almeno una buona notizia c'è: l'edizione originale del gioco è tornata in vendita.

La questione commerciale era stata un'altra fonte di polemiche. Al lancio della Complete Edition, Sega aveva anche rimosso dalla vendita le versioni originali di Shogun 2, costringendo di fatto i nuovi giocatori a scegliere la nuova edizione, più costosa e contestata. È importante precisare che chi possedeva già il titolo originale poteva continuare ad accedervi, ma per tutti gli altri non c'era alternativa alla remaster.

items.title: Meta e Apple tornano a lavorare assieme: merito dell'AI
items.summary: Il nuovo modello open multimodale Muse Spark da ben 816 miliardi di parametri può essere eseguito completamente in locale, con due Mac Studio basati su M5 Ultra.
items.content:
Meta ha annunciato nelle scorse ore Muse Spark Open, un nuovo modello AI open-weight che l'azienda definisce il più capace mai sviluppato negli Stati Uniti in questa categoria. Una delle caratteristiche principali è la possibilità di eseguirlo totalmente in locale su un computer desktop, per la precisione due Mac Studio con chip Apple M5 Ultra e il framework MLX aggiornato. Il modello rappresenta anche l'inizio di collaborazione pubblica tra Meta e Apple, due aziende che spesso si trovano in competizione nel settore tech - e altrettanto spesso hanno dimostrato di essere in forte disaccordo l'una con l'altra.

In questo caso, però, i vertici delle due società hanno confermato il lavoro congiunto e si sono pure scambiati messaggi di apprezzamento sui social; Mark Zuckerberg ha annunciato su X che i pesi di Muse Spark Open sono disponibili da oggi e ha sottolineato che il modello funziona bene sui nuovi Mac Studio grazie al lavoro svolto insieme a John Ternus, nuovo CEO della Mela, e al resto del team. Ternus ha risposto congratulandosi con il team di Meta che si è occupato dello sviluppo del modello, sottolineando la possibilità di eseguire un modello di questa portata in modo efficiente direttamente da un sistema desktop, senza bisogno di fare ricorso al cloud.

items.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.mercor.com/research/labor-index/benchmark-map/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50121179 Points: 374 # Comments: 322
items.content:
AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. This Benchmark Map is our first step toward building a comprehensive, continuously updated resource for understanding AI capabilities across the economy.

Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.

In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts , and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.

Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.

The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:

For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.

As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.

To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.

To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:

Following work by Wang et al. , we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.

To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al. ’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.

A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.

Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.

We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).

By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.

Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.

The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al. ), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.

But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:

After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:

The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.

Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.

We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.

O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average , we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.

As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:

In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal.

However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain:

The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores.

Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality.

In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction , but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive.

Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks.

items.title: Hyundai IONIQ 3 punta al titolo di Auto Europa 2027: è tra le sette finaliste
items.summary: Hyundai IONIQ 3 è tra le sette finaliste di Auto Europa 2027. La compatta elettrica offre fino a 497 km WLTP, 441 litri di bagagliaio e PLEOS Connect
items.content:
La nuova Hyundai IONIQ 3 entra in un gruppo ristretto e speciale: quello delle sette finaliste del Premio Auto Europa 2027, il riconoscimento promosso dall'Unione Italiana Giornalisti Automotive (UIGA). La compatta alla spina ha superato la prima selezione effettuata dai giornalisti dell'associazione e dalla giuria degli Opinion Leader, conquistando l'accesso alla fase conclusiva.La candidatura pone sotto i riflettori un modello importante per la strategia europea di Hyundai. Con IONIQ 3, infatti, il costruttore porta la propria famiglia di elettriche nel segmento B, facendo leva su dimensioni contenute, autonomia competitiva e soluzioni tecnologiche solitamente associate a veicoli di categoria superiore.

Una compatta progettata per l'Europa

La IONIQ 3 nasce da un progetto portato avanti per soddisfare le pretese del mercato europeo. Non a caso sarà prodotta nello stabilimento Hyundai Motor Türkiye di Ä°zmit, in Turchia.Sul piano stilistico, la vettura introduce la silhouette denominata Aero Hatch, espressione della filosofia di design "Art of Steel". Le forme sono state pensate per esaltare il carattere e il rendimento aerodinamico, pur senza sacrificare la praticità richiesta a un'automobile destinata all'utilizzo di tutti i giorni.Particolarmente affascinante è il rapporto tra ingombri esterni e abitabilità. Il passo di 2.680 mm, abbinato al pavimento piatto, permette di sfruttare in modo efficace lo spazio disponibile per i passeggeri, avvicinando la sistemazione interna a quella di alcuni modelli del segmento C.Inoltre, il bagagliaio offre una capacità complessiva di 441 litri, un valore significativo per una hatchback di questa categoria. Hyundai sottolinea, tra le varie cose, il livello raggiunto dall'insonorizzazione, elemento che contribuisce al comfort durante gli spostamenti.

Due batterie e fino a 497 chilometri WLTP

La gamma prevede due differenti capacità della batteria. La versione con accumulatore da 61 kWh dichiara fino a 497 km di autonomia nel ciclo combinato WLTP, mentre quella da 42,2 kWh raggiunge un massimo di 344 chilometri. Sono valori omologati, naturalmente differenti dalle percorrenze effettive che possono variare in funzione della temperatura, della velocità e delle condizioni di utilizzo.Per quanto riguarda il rifornimento di energia, Hyundai indica un tempo di circa 30 minuti per passare dal 10 all'80% della carica in condizioni ottimali. È prevista anche la possibilità di utilizzare un caricatore trifase in corrente alternata da 22 kW, soluzione utile soprattutto presso le infrastrutture pubbliche compatibili.Non manca la tecnologia Vehicle-to-Load (V2L), che consente di alimentare dispositivi elettrici esterni sfruttando l'energia immagazzinata nella batteria dell'automobile.

Debutta PLEOS Connect con intelligenza artificiale

Passi avanti importanti anche per quanto concerne l'infotainment. IONIQ 3 introduce sul mercato europeo PLEOS Connect, il sistema Hyundai basato su Android Automotive OS, con uno schermo che può raggiungere i 14,6 pollici.La piattaforma supporta aggiornamenti software OTA, che consentono di intervenire su determinate funzionalità senza passare necessariamente dall'officina. L'interazione con il veicolo viene inoltre arricchita da Gleo AI, l'assistente intelligente sviluppato per rendere più naturale l'utilizzo dei servizi digitali.L'insieme di queste caratteristiche contribuisce a spiegare la presenza della vettura tra le candidate al premio UIGA, che valorizza le novità più significative per il mercato automobilistico europeo. Vedremo se la compatta coreana riuscirà a succedere alla Fiat Grande Panda, che riuscì a ottenere il riconoscimento lo scorso anno.[drivek_widget brand_id="hyundai" model_id="kona"]

items.title: Deputato legge il discorso dagli occhiali smart: scoppia il caso
items.summary: Un deputato gallese usa gli occhiali smart come gobbo e scatena una polemica sulla privacy.
items.content:
Gli occhiali intelligenti stanno diventando così discreti da poter essere scambiati per normali montature da vista, se non fosse per il led, che però si attiva solo quando stiamo scattando una foto o giriamo un video. E poi alcuni modelli integrano piccoli display capaci di mostrare messaggi, traduzioni e persino interi discorsi davanti agli occhi.

Essendo tecnologia relativamente nuova, le possibili implicazioni sono tute da scoprire, ma un piccolo assaggio arriva dall'UK. In effetti, dispositivi simili potrebbero cambiare il modo di comunicare in pubblico, ma quando accadono episodi come quello di cui vi vogliamo raccontare, e che riguardano le istituzioni, appare evidente che ne vedremo delle belle in futuro.

La dimostrazione arriva dal Galles, dove Jason O'Connell, esponente di Reform UK, è finito al centro di una polemica dopo un intervento al Senedd, il Parlamento gallese, lo scorso 30 settembre. Per circa cinque minuti il politico ha snocciolato statistiche e argomentazioni contro il limite di velocità di 32 km/h senza apparentemente consultare alcun appunto.

items.title: Tesla Roadster, Elon Musk svela negli Stati Uniti l'auto che vola
items.summary: Il lancio-show dell'ultima nata Tesla nella sede di SpaceX
items.content:
Elon Musk presenta Roadster , la sua prima auto volante. Equipaggiata con razzi SpaceX , la vettura può spiccare il volo e lo ha fatto durante il suo lancio. È salita su una rampa curva e poi si è lanciata, atterrando in modo controllato grazie ai suoi propulsori. Per sorprendere ancora di più i presenti, l'auto ha anche saltato cinque veicoli parcheggiati esibendosi in una piroetta in aria.

"Abbiamo bisogno del pubblico per dimostrare che non si tratta di intelligenza artificiale o di superintelligenza. Quello che vedete è il risultato della collaborazione fra la migliore casa automobilistica e la migliore società di razzi", ha detto Elon Musk, presentando l'ultima nata in casa Tesla.

Capace di effettuare in aria manovre precluse alle automobili fino ad ora, su strada la Tesla Roadster si annuncia altrettanto impressionante, visto che la variante Rocket impiega meno di 0,59 secondi per raggiungere una velocità di quasi 100 km/h. Oltre al modello più estremo che può sollevarsi da terra ed ha una configurazione monoposto, in gamma ci saranno anche le varianti Performance e Thrust. La prima, a due posti, scatta da fermo fino a quasi 100 km/h in meno di 1,6 secondi e si avvale di un sistema di aspirazione nel sottoscocca per aumentare l'aderenza. La seconda, invece, è dotata di propulsori posteriori con cui può ridurre il tempo di accelerazione da 0 fino a 100 km/h a meno di 0,9 secondi. Sempre parlando di numeri, la Tesla Roadster sarà in grado, secondo la casa, di superare i 370 km/h e di offrire un'autonomia superiore a 480 chilometri. Al momento non sono stati comunicati i prezzi della vettura, che dovrebbe andare in produzione, secondo le previsioni di Tesla, nel 2028.

Il lancio è avvenuto nella sede di SpaceX , in un'atmosfera da concerto all'aperto, davanti a una folla di appassionati che, nove anni fa, ha versato 250.000 dollari per prenotare l'auto appena presentata e che dovrà ancora attendere prima di poterla guidare. La vettura entrerà infatti in produzione nel 2028.

"Questo è il culmine dell'incredibile lavoro degli ingegneri di Tesla e SpaceX per creare qualcosa che non avete mai visto neanche nei film, qualcosa di meglio di un'auto di James Bond", ha detto un orgoglioso Musk durante l'evento. La vettura è considerata da molti una mossa di Musk per attirare l'attenzione sul potenziale di una fusione fra Tesla e SpaceX, alla quale l'uomo più ricco del mondo aspira.

"È stata una dimostrazione di forza ingegneristica priva di valore commerciale, se non quello di mettere in imbarazzo le case automobilistiche tradizionali", ha affermato Gene Munster, managing partner di Deepwater Asset Management, società che investe in Tesla, aggiungendo che la presentazione ha inviato un chiaro segnale: Musk non vede l'ora di unire Tesla e SpaceX.

items.title: Anna's Archive, la shadow library segnalata dalla RIAA al governo USA
items.summary: La shadow library che copiò il database di Spotify è stata aggiunta alla "entity list" di pirateria e contraffazione.
items.content:
La RIAA (Recording Industry Association of America) ha chiesto agli Stati Uniti di includere nuovi servizi online nella lista delle entità note per la pirateria e la contraffazione: è un documento ufficiale presentato ogni anno allo United States Trade Representative (USTR). La lista dell'USTR ha una funzione principalmente dissuasiva: non costituisce una sentenza e non determina automaticamente l'illegalità dei servizi inclusi. L'obiettivo è richiamare l'attenzione sulle piattaforme considerate problematiche e spingere le autorità e i Paesi interessati a intensificare controlli e indagini nei loro confronti.

Le principali "new entry" sono due, e probabilmente non a sorpresa per chi ha seguito un po' la vicenda, la prima è Anna's Archive. La cosiddetta shadow library è finita negli scorsi mesi al centro di una colossale controversia legale con Spotify e le principali etichette discografiche per aver copiato e pubblicato su Torrent la stragrande maggioranza dell'intero catalogo della piattaforma di streaming. Per la precisione, un database da 86 milioni di file musicali e metadati relativi a 256 milioni di tracce.

La notizia aveva provocato una reazione legale immediata da parte dell'industria musicale. Pochi giorni dopo, la RIAA aveva coordinato un'azione giudiziaria d'urgenza per conto dei propri membri e di Spotify. la vicenda è stata abbastanza articolata ma, semplificando moltissimo, la coalizione di Spotify ha vinto al 100%; non che ci fossero grossi dubbi a riguardo, oggettivamente, ma del resto Anna's Archive non si è nemmeno presentata in aula - comprensibilmente, visto che i loro gestori sono anonimi e non sono stati individuati. In ultimo la vittoria in tribunale è stata più di forma che altro: le major non hanno incassato il risarcimento centimilionario accordato dal giudice, né hanno ottenuto la messa offline del sito. Certo, hanno bloccato alcuni domini, ma la shadow library si è semplicemente trasferita in altri domini su cui gli USA non hanno alcuna giurisdizione.

items.title: Giornalista del Washington Post ferita dai coloni in Cisgiordania: "Mi hanno spinto a terra e preso a calci"
items.summary: La fotoreporter Heidi Levine sarebbe stata ripresa mentre veniva picchiata durante uno scontro tra coloni e palestinesi. Netanyahu: 'Israele condanna ma fatti poco chiari'
items.content:
Il media palestinese Quds riferisce su X che la giornalista americana del Washington Post Heidi Levine è rimasta ferita in seguito ad un'aggressione da parte di coloni israeliani estremisti mentre documentava la raccolta delle olive nel villaggio di Abu Falah, a nord di Ramallah . Quds ha postato la foto della giornalista in ospedale.

La fotoreporter sarebbe stata ripresa, scrive il Times of Israel, oggi mentre veniva picchiata con dei bastoni da coloni mascherati durante un violento scontro tra coloni e palestinesi avvenuto durante la raccolta delle olive vicino al villaggio di Abu Falah. Il filmato dell'incidente, pubblicato su X da attivisti internazionali al seguito dei palestinesi, mostra coloni e palestinesi che si lanciano pietre a vicenda, mentre si sentono spari provenienti da una fonte non identificata. La fotoreporter, che secondo quanto riferito ha circa sessant'anni, viene ripresa mentre giace a terra e viene picchiata con dei bastoni da alcuni individui mascherati, che poi si danno alla fuga. Altri giornalisti e palestinesi si avvicinano a lei, e la si sente dire in inglese: "Non sto bene. Mi hanno portato via tutte le mie cose".

"Sono stato aggredita, spinta a terra. Per fortuna avevo il giubbotto antiproiettile e l'elmetto, altrimenti probabilmente non sarei nemmeno qui, perché continuavano a prendermi a calci" . Lo ha raccontato ai colleghi di Reuters, che lo scrivono sul sito, la fotoreporter del Washington Post Heidi Levine ferita questa mattina in un attacco di un gruppo di coloni estremisti israeliani vicino al villaggio di Abu Falah, a nord di Ramallah, mentre documentava la raccolta di olive degli agricoltori palestinesi. Levine è stata ricoverata in ospedale a Ramallah.

"I fatti relativi allo scontro avvenuto vicino ad Abu Falah, durante il quale la fotoreporter del Washington Post Heidi Levin sarebbe stata aggredita, sono ancora poco chia ri e sono oggetto di indagine. Israele condanna inequivocabilmente la violenza contro qualsiasi persona. Tuttavia, rimangono importanti interrogativi". Lo scrive l'ufficio del premier Benyamin Netanyahu su X. "Secondo quanto riportato, circa 200 arabi e attivisti di estrema sinistra si sono scontrati con circa 40 giovani israeliani. I filmati mostrano persone mascherate da entrambe le parti che lanciano oggetti, insieme a segnalazioni di fuochi d'artificio sparati contro giovani ebrei. In altri filmati, sembra che Levin sia stata spinta a terra e subito dopo la stessa persona, la cui identità è sconosciuta, l'abbia aiutata a rialzarsi. L'indagine deve accertare i fatti, compreso chi ha iniziato la violenza".

items.title: Diego Poncelet è lo skateboarder più veloce della storia
items.summary: L'atleta Red Bull ha stabilito un nuovo Guinness World Record™ raggiungendo i 151,83 km/h
items.content:
Diego Poncelet è lo skateboarder più veloce della storia. L'atleta Red Bull, spagnolo, 27 anni, due volte campione del mondo di downhill skateboarding, ha raggiunto i 151,83 km/h (94,34 mph) sulla Route du Port di Les Éboulements, in Québec (Canada), conquistando il titolo Guinness World Records™ per la velocità più alta mai raggiunta su uno skateboard in posizione eretta. La discesa, su un tratto di strada chiuso al traffico, è stata certificata da un giudice ufficiale Guinness World Records il 22 settembre 2026.

Già nel primo giorno di prove Poncelet aveva superato i 146,73 km/h di Pete Connolly, primato imbattuto dal 2017 e stabilito sulla stessa collina, toccando i 146,88 km/h. Le condizioni di vento lo hanno però costretto ad attendere cinque giorni la finestra giusta: con una coda di vento di 10-14 km/h da nord-est è tornato in strada e ha portato il limite oltre i 150 km/h. Il risultato arriva al termine di anni di preparazione tra aerodinamica, condizione fisica, sviluppo dell'attrezzatura e meteorologia. "A 146,88 km/h non ero ancora soddisfatto. Solo quando ho toccato i 151 km/h ho provato una gioia totale", racconta Diego Poncelet. Con determinazione, innovazione e anni di preparazione, Diego Poncelet ha trasformato un sogno di una vita in un nuovo record mondiale, diventando lo skateboarder più veloce della storia. items.title: MSI, arriva la GeForce RTX 5080 dedicata a Call of Duty MW4
items.summary: Solo una livrea speciale o c'è anche della sostanza?
items.content:
Proprio in questi giorni in cui si ipotizza che NVIDIA abbia deciso di gettare la spugna sulle GeForce RTX 5090, MSI ha presentato una nuova scheda grafica di fascia alta in edizione limitata, e guarda caso è una RTX 5080. Per la precisione è la MSI GeForce RTX 5080 16G COD MW4 EDITION OC, chiaramente dedicata all'ultimo capitolo del franchise di FPS militari di Activision. Le vendite della scheda partiranno il 23 ottobre, proprio lo stesso giorno di rilascio del gioco.

La caratteristica più evidente della nuova scheda è la livrea custom: su tutta la scocca possiamo osservare diversi dettagli gialli, compreso il sistema di raffreddamento, mentre il backplate include una sezione trasparente che lascia intravedere parte del PCB, che fa sempre scena. Sulla stessa superficie trova spazio anche un ritratto di Ghost, uno dei personaggi più riconoscibili dell'intero universo di Call of Duty. MSI sottolinea che le illustrazioni sono state sviluppate appositamente per questa collaborazione.

Il sistema dissipazione è il classico TRIO FROZR 4 già visto su altre schede di fascia alta del produttore. Il dissipatore comprende ventole STORMFORCE con pale decorate con una particolare texture a forma di artiglio, e una base in rame nichelato. La struttura integra inoltre le tecnologie Wave Curved 4.0 e Air Antegrade Fin 2.0, progettate per ottimizzare il flusso d'aria attraverso il dissipatore. MSI, tuttavia, non ha ancora pubblicato misurazioni delle temperature o dei livelli acustici, quindi non è possibile stabilire se questa edizione offra vantaggi concreti rispetto alle altre RTX 5080 del produttore.

items.title: Yellowjackets, la quarta stagione arriva il 20 novembre su Paramount+
items.summary: Le sopravvissute tornano a casa nel teaser dell'ultima stagione, in arrivo il 20 novembre.
items.content:
Il ritorno alla normalità può essere persino più difficile della lotta per sopravvivere, ed è proprio su questo contrasto che si concentra l'ultimo capitolo di Yellowjackets, la serie thriller che ha conquistato il pubblico mescolando horror psicologico, mistero e dramma adolescenziale. La quarta e ultima stagione debutterà su Paramount+ il 20 novembre 2026, come confermato dal nuovo teaser ufficiale.

Dopo aver trascorso mesi nelle terre selvagge del Nord America, le protagoniste riescono finalmente a tornare a casa. Ma il loro incubo è tutt'altro che concluso. Le immagini diffuse dalla piattaforma anticipano un ritorno segnato dai traumi e dalle conseguenze delle terribili decisioni prese per sopravvivere.

Per chi non conoscesse la serie, Yellowjackets racconta la storia di una squadra femminile di calcio liceale, il cui aereo precipita in una regione isolata. Quella che inizialmente sembra una disperata lotta contro la fame e il freddo si trasforma progressivamente in qualcosa di molto più inquietante, tra rivalità, violenza e comportamenti sempre più estremi. La particolarità della produzione, creata da Ashley Lyle e Bart Nickerson, è la sua struttura narrativa. Gli eventi del passato si intrecciano con quelli ambientati quasi 25 anni dopo, mostrando come le protagoniste adulte continuino a convivere con segreti e sensi di colpa.

items.title: Sommerso e illegale valgono 218 miliardi, il 9,9% del Pil
items.summary: Lo scatto Istat sul 2024. Cresce il lavoro irregolare, 3,2 milioni di unità
items.content:
Un tesoro che sfugge a fisco, previdenza e contratti ed un mercato parallelo tra traffico di droga, prostituzione e contrabbando di sigarette. L'Italia che viaggia in ombra non arretra: sommerso e attività illegali valgono nel 2024 oltre 218 miliardi di euro. Sono gli ultimi dati che l'Istat mette nero su bianco nel report sull'economia non osservata. E a finire sotto la lente in particolare è la crescita del lavoro irregolare: un fenomeno che arriva a riguardare oltre 3,2 milioni di unità. Una piaga che si allarga, incidendo su tutele, salari e contributi. Il quadro è, dunque, quello dei grandi numeri. In totale il valore dell'economia non osservata nel 2024 si attesta a 218,2 miliardi, in aumento dello 0,3% rispetto al 2023 (quando era a 217,6 miliardi), a fronte di una crescita del Pil corrente del 3,2%.

La sua incidenza sul Pil scende così al 9,9% dal 10,2% dell'anno precedente. Il bottino più consistente fa capo all'economia sommersa che sale a 198,4 miliardi, mentre il valore delle attività illegali scende a 19,8 miliardi. A sostenere la dinamica complessiva è proprio la crescita del valore aggiunto connesso all'impiego di lavoro irregolare, che aumenta del 3,9% (corrispondente a circa 3,1 miliardi). Questa la dimensione dei fenomeni: il lavoro irregolare e la sotto-dichiarazione di fatturato e/o costi delle imprese arrivano ad un valore di 187,8 miliardi.

Marcata, invece, la contrazione di altre componenti del sommerso: mance e fitti non dichiarati diminuiscono del 13,1% (pari a -1,6 miliardi) rispetto al 2023. Risultato: l'occupazione non in regola continua a crescere in Italia ad un ritmo superiore rispetto a quella in regola. Portando con sé un'evasione fiscale e contributiva. I dati Istat dicono che le unità di lavoro irregolari raggiungono quota 3 milioni e 277mila - di cui 2 milioni e 396mila unità sono dipendenti - con un aumento di 145mila rispetto al 2023 (+4,6%): quasi tre volte la crescita registrata dal lavoro regolare (+1,6%). "È un segnale che dovrebbe spingerci a guardare non soltanto al numero degli occupati, ma anche alle condizioni nelle quali si lavora", commenta il presidente di Adapt, Francesco Seghezzi. Numeri che, per la Cgil, "certificano il fallimento della strategia portata avanti in questi anni dal governo. Serve un cambio radicale", chiede il sindacato, calcolando l'impatto sulle persone: "Poiché si tratta di unità di lavoro standard, ciò significa che, in termini di donne e uomini in carne e ossa, parliamo di almeno 4 milioni di persone".

La crescita riguarda in particolare il settore delle costruzioni, l'agricoltura e si concentra soprattutto nei servizi alle persone. Non manca il peso delle attività illegali, che resta consistente ma si ridimensiona. Nel 2024 il traffico di stupefacenti registra una lieve riduzione e il suo valore scende a 14,9 miliardi di euro. Nello stesso periodo, invece, i servizi di prostituzione mostrano una crescita e valgono 4,2 miliardi. Mentre si conferma marginale l'attività di contrabbando di sigarette con un valore a 0,6 miliardi. "Una battaglia dimenticata e persa, quella contro l'evasione, che resta una voragine, un problema irrisolto di questo Paese. Non parliamo poi del lavoro nero che spopola", afferma il presidente dell'Unione nazionale consumatori, Massimiliano Dona. "La bassa crescita del Prodotto interno lordo poggia sulle paghe da miseria ai lavoratori, sul mancato versamento di contributi all'Inps e su tasse non pagate", attacca Osvaldo Napoli, della direzione nazionale di Azione.

items.title: JPEG XL vs. AVIF for web use-cases
items.summary: Article URL: https://jakearchibald.com/2026/jpeg-xl-vs-avif/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50120224 Points: 184 # Comments: 142
items.content:
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data .

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data .

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data .

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself .

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples .

JPEG XL can make existing JPEGs 9–20% smaller, without further loss. It's also as fast or faster to decode, except for small images. See the data .

For lossless, JPEG XL is the clear winner. Lossless WebP is 9–17% larger for photos, and lossless AVIF is 30–120% larger. But lossless images are almost never what you want on the web. If you do use them on the web (like I do on this page), watch out for jixel's higher efforts - it often produces files that are too slow to decode. See the data .

Animated image formats continue to be a dumb idea. Please don't use them. Learn more , if you must.

For web use-cases, I'd currently default to AVIF 4:4:4, with the highest effort level I can be bothered with. If I felt AVIF was producing an unusually large file, I'd take a look at JPEG XL via jixel, and see if it did better.

Both AVIF and JPEG XL (via jixel) have seen massive improvements recently, so it's possible that this recommendation could change in future. There's been a lot of misinformation around this stuff, and your AI will happily deliver that misinformation to you. Instead, test things with your own images.

AVIF folks suggest that JPEG XL is technically limited compared to AVIF. That might be true, but in this article I'm focusing on results with today's implementations.

I 'created' a benchmarking script , that encodes images using various codecs at various settings, and records various details.

I'm using the latest released versions of the image codecs, which at time of writing is:

I chose a selection of images, and encoded most of them to a width of 1598 pixels - which is 2x the maximum width images appear on this blog. This means they look sharp on high density displays , which most users have. As a result, if you're viewing this on a small or low density screen, you're not getting the full experience.

When I first wrote about AVIF , I used an F1 car as the first image, so I figured I'd do that again!

I encoded the image at various codec qualities, and chose versions that were closest to particular SSIMULACRA2 scores - a perceptual image quality metric by the folks behind JPEG XL. 50 is considered medium quality, 70 high, 80 very high, and 90 visually lossless. Although, I'm not sure if these ratings take high density displays into account.

Throughout the article, the visual comparisons, like above, use each encoder's maximum effort, except in cases where maximum effort results in a larger file (yes, that happens).

For archival, I'd tend towards near-lossless qualities, but if I'm just displaying an illustrative image on my blog, performance is more important to me. I'm personally happy with the 70 result above. If you zoom in, you can see the quality loss, but if I was really concerned about the zoom-in case, I'd use something like the VisualViewport API to load in a higher resolution image when that happens, rather than make the download bigger for everyone.

At lower qualities you can see the difference in strategy between the codecs. The detail loss is around the same, but AVIF tends to smooth things out compared to the original, whereas JPEG XL seems to introduce rougher patterns.

Also, I feel that, at medium quality (50), the AVIF and libjxl look better than the jixel version. The jixel version has a lot of visible noise around the BWT logo, and the Microsoft text on the front wing is way less legible. It makes me wonder about the metric a bit.

There's going to be a lot of these graphs, so here's what's going on:

Here are the quality results using a different quality metric, ColorVideoVDP :

The result is roughly the same except this metric puts more of a gap between AVIF and the JPEG XL images.

It also suggests there's some advantage to AVIF with 4:2:0 chroma subsampling at lower qualities, but it's minor.

When it comes to images on my blog, I encode with maximum effort settings. I'm happy to wait a couple of seconds to get an image that's faster to load for every user. However, if you're doing a lot of encoding on a server, encode time becomes more of a concern.

Another thing that might be a concern if you're encoding images on a server is peak memory usage:

It's worth considering decoding performance. If decoding is particularly slow, then it might make the file size benefit less valuable, especially when images are loaded from a cache.

JPEG XL becomes suddenly faster to decode at very high quality settings (but still slower than AVIF). I think this is due to an edge preserving filter that does more work at lower quality settings.

I've heard people say that AVIF's tendency to smooth out details makes it bad for human faces, so I picked this image from Unsplash .

At lower qualities, you can see the smoothing on the face, but it's the same for both AVIF and JPEG XL.

It's interesting that, at lower qualities, jixel decodes much slower in Safari.

I threw this one in because it's the default image in Squoosh , but I guess the sharp lines of the hairs make it different to the previous images. In fact, even at medium quality, the difference from the original is much less perceptible to my eyes compared to the other images.

items.title: Linux su PS5, grandi progressi per le console con jailbreak
items.summary: Ora è possibile installare il sistema operativo open-source su console con praticamente tutti i firmware, tranne gli ultimissimi due.
items.content:
La scena homebrew di PlayStation 5 compie un nuovo passo avanti con pLinux5-NG, uno dei progetti più interessanti da seguire per quanto riguarda l'installazione di Linux sulle console di Sony (con jailbreak, naturalmente). Il nuovo bootloader permette infatti di avviare distro Linux anche su sistemi aggiornati fino al firmware 13.60, superando il limite precedente: il software è ancora in fase di test, ma potrebbe rendere la PS5 una piattaforma più versatile - non solo per Linux in generale, ma anche per eseguire applicazioni e giochi per PC.

Il precedente bootloader ps5-linux funzionava sulle console con firmware compreso tra le versioni 3.00 e 7.61. Per testare Linux era quindi necessario disporre di una PS5 che non fosse mai stata aggiornata dopo agosto 2023. Con pLinux5-NG, il requisito cambia: il supporto si estende a tutte le console eccezion fatta per quelle che montano i due ultimissimi firmware originale, ovvero il 14.00 e il 14.10, distribuiti rispettivamente a settembe e ottobre 2026. Gli sviluppatori hanno confermato i progressi attraverso la pagina GitHub del progetto, mentre sui social sono già apparse dimostrazioni dell'avvio di distro popolari come Ubuntu e CachyOS.

Il processo richiede l'impiego dell'exploit Relapse e di Byepervisor-Reborn, strumenti che permettono di aggirare alcune delle protezioni di sicurezza implementate da Sony. Queste tecniche sono estremamente popolari nella community di questi tempi, anche perché possono essere sfruttate per eseguire copie pirata dei videogiochi, oltre che per attività legittime di ricerca e sviluppo homebrew. Naturalmente le implicazioni in ambito PC gaming derivano da SteamOS, che appunto è basato su Linux, e Proton, il layer di compatibilità sviluppato da Valve che permette di eseguire i giochi del catalogo Steam compilati originariamente per Windows sul sistema open-source.
